question.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}
$$
